item.title: The multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier
item.description: arXiv:2611.15992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier is six, giving a structural, enumeration-free lower-bound proof valid against unrestricted nonlinear reuse in Boolean XOR-AND circuits. The value was previously established by SAT searches of the second author. An explicit six-AND circuit supplies the upper bound. The lower bound combines derivatives, quadratic products, complementary minors, and extraction modulo a Boolean ideal. Independent finite checks accompany the arguments. $\mathrm{MC}(M_3)=6$ is fully formalized in Lean 4. The kernel-checked proof uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
item.dc:creator: Bshara Alhodali, Gregory Morse

item.title: The Ultimate Karp-Lipton Collapse
item.description: arXiv:2611.16096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Karp and Lipton proved that if $NP\subseteq P/poly$, then $PH$ collapses. A long line of work pushed the collapse to smaller classes. In particular, Chakaravarthy and Roy obtained two such collapses, to (apparently) incomparable classes $O_2^P$ and $P^{prMA}$. We united them earlier by a collapse to the input-oblivious version $P^{prOMA}$ of $P^{prMA}$, which is contained in both; and, jointly with Williams, to a slightly smaller class. Two other deepest known collapses are to $ZPP^{ONP}$ (following from K\"obler and Watanabe) and to $OL_2^P$ (proved in this paper). We unite the three collapses by a collapse to a class contained in all of them. We use a three-stage computational model OGTD (oblivious generator-tester-decoder): a polynomial-time generator with an oracle computes an advice string from $1^n$, a tester certifies it, and a polynomial-time decoder uses it (it is the only one that sees the actual input). Let $OM$ be the class of OGTD languages defined by a restricted version of $prOMA$ as the generator's oracle, by a co-$ONP$ tester, and a $P$ decoder. We show that it is contained in the three collapse classes above and prove that $PH$ collapses to $OM$ under $NP\subseteq P/poly$. The collapse also holds for an unambiguous version of $OM$. All these input-oblivious collapse classes lie in $P^{prSBP}$, and so do even the non-input-oblivious versions $P^{prMA}$, $L_2^P$ and $S_2^P$: we prove that $P^{prS_2^P}\subseteq P^{prSBP}$. This strengthens the containment $S_2^P\subseteq P^{prAM}$ of Chakaravarthy and Roy and our earlier containment $L_2^P\subseteq P^{prSBP}$. The proof unites the Goldreich-Wigderson-type procedure of Chakaravarthy and Roy with our earlier approximate-counting technique. Its input-oblivious counterpart concerns $O_2^P$, the first collapse class of Chakaravarthy and Roy: every language in $O_2^P$ has polynomial-size circuits constructible in $FP^{prSBP}$.
item.dc:creator: Edward A. Hirsch (Ariel University), Ilya Volkovich (Boston College)

item.title: Weak Composition Theorems for Randomized Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.16192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present two results towards the randomized communication complexity of composed functions. Our contributions include: - \textbf{Lifting-by-Influence.} For any binary function $f$ and any outer gadget $g:\{0,1\}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we show that up to additive terms, computing $g \circ f^n$ information-theoretically requires solving at least $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ instances of $f$, where $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ denotes the total influence of $g$. To our knowledge, this is the first composition lower bound for randomized communication that applies to \emph{every} choice of $f$ and $g$. - \textbf{Symmetric Composition.} When $g$ is a symmetric function with a value transition at Hamming weight $d$, we strengthen the number of required instances to $\min\{d,n+1-d\}$. As an implication, this recovers the previously known direct-sum theorem, XOR lemma, and majority lemma. Our proofs develop novel and distinctive usages of the classical \emph{input embedding} argument of Barak, Braverman, Chen, and Rao (SICOMP 2013). As an additional ingredient, we introduce a new public sampling framework that avoids auxiliary communication during the recovery phase of the protocol, ultimately reducing the extra cost from $O(n)$ bits of information to just $O(1)$.
item.dc:creator: Pachara Sawettamalya

item.title: Exact Quantum Algorithms for Composed Boolean Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.16412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study exact quantum algorithms for block compositions of total Boolean functions. For an outer function $f$ of degree $D$ and an inner function $g$ on $m$ bits, we prove $$ Q_E(f\circ g)=O\!\left(mD+Q_E(f)Q_{1/(4D)}(g)\right). $$ The algorithm combines approximate inner evaluations with a finite exact correction. Its two costs are governed by different parameters of the outer function: exact query complexity determines the cost of simulation, whereas polynomial degree determines the number of inner blocks used in the correction. We first establish the construction with an arity-dependent error threshold and then obtain the degree-dependent threshold above. For recursive ternary not-all-equal, this gives an exact algorithm using $(3/\sqrt2)^{k(1+o(1))}$ queries asymptotically. More generally, for every fixed nonconstant total gadget $h$, we determine the exact recursive rate as $\max\{\textrm{deg}(h),\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(h)\}$ and prove $Q_E(h^{\circ k})=\widetilde O_h(R(h^{\circ k})^2)$. The composition limit also allows to transfer separations from $Q_{\varepsilon}$ and $\deg$ to exact quantum query complexity $Q_E$ (similar to fractional block sensitivity to block sensitivity transfer in Tal and Kulkarni 2016, Chicago Journal of Theoretical Computer Science). We construct a family with $s=\operatorname{bs}=\operatorname{fbs}\ge Q_E^{3/2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $1.1527\ldots$. A second construction gives $R \ge Q_E^{2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $3/2$. We also allow different inner functions and give analogous quantitative separations in quantum communication.
item.dc:creator: Gagan Chiruvella, Chandrima Kayal, Rajat Mittal, Manaswi Paraashar, Nitin Saurabh

item.title: Topological Entropy of Group Cellular Automata is Effectively Computable
item.description: arXiv:2611.16746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological entropy is a fundamental invariant of dynamical systems, quantifying their complexity. For cellular automata, however, determining topological entropy is generally algorithmically intractable. We study group cellular automata, namely cellular automata over a finite group alphabet whose global map is a group endomorphism. In dimension one, we decompose topological entropy into two one-sided components describing information propagating from the left and from the right in space--time. We introduce finite families of left and right traces and prove that the entropy is the sum of their growth rates. Hence, the entropy is completely determined by the growth rate of a fixed-width family of space--time patterns. This reduction from arbitrarily large windows to uniformly bounded width yields an effective procedure for computing the entropy. In particular, the entropy of every one-dimensional group cellular automaton is the logarithm of a positive integer. Using Pontryagin duality and the Bridge Theorem between topological and algebraic entropy, we also derive an explicit formula for linear cellular automata over $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$ in terms of their characteristic polynomial. Moreover, in every dimension $D\geq 2$, a group cellular automaton is either equicontinuous with zero entropy or sensitive to initial conditions with infinite entropy. Combined with decidability of equicontinuity, this implies that topological entropy is effectively computable from the local rule in every dimension. Thus, group cellular automata form a natural nontrivial class in which algebraic structure restores computability of topological entropy.
item.dc:creator: Niccol\`o Castronuovo, Alberto Dennunzio, Jarkko Kari, Luciano Margara

item.title: Computation with Backward Feedback: Power, Observation, and Cost
item.description: arXiv:2611.16779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much can a computation gain by passing information back to an earlier stage, and how soon can an observer obtain the answer? We study deterministic programs whose runs are accessed at randomly selected stages. A program keeps a register, a finite block of memory. A random clock selects the current stage; each tick takes a random step, with a law fixed independently of input, program and register. When the clock moves backward, the register contents at the stage it leaves start a new run, and the clock continues where it lands. Equilibrium readout requires a distribution of clock position and register that one tick leaves unchanged, and a correct final answer under every such distribution. For bounded steps in both directions with negative average, we obtain an exact classification at each polynomial scale s. If running time and register length are both O(s), feedback gives exactly nondeterministic space O(s); without transmission the class is deterministic time O(s), which is strictly smaller. An observer that starts at stage zero with an all-zero register, reads sequentially and never accepts a nonmember sees, with fewer ticks than any exponential, only languages fixed by a bounded input prefix. Exponentially many ticks reveal every linear-time language. For a clock moving one step up or down, we bound the wait for useful backward moves and the rate of random erasures a stored counter tolerates. The results separate the power of feedback at equilibrium, observation from a fixed start, and the cost of obtaining and keeping information.
item.dc:creator: Saman Farhat, Farzad Didehvar

item.title: Sowing the Seeds of Intractability: Kalah is PSPACE-complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.17252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kalah is a classic two-player game in the mancala family of sowing games. Computers have solved several standard-size starting positions, but the complexity of the game on boards of growing size has remained open. We study the natural generalization in which the number of pits per side is part of the input and an arbitrary position is given, with the stone counts given in unary. We show that deciding whether a designated player can force a win from such a position is PSPACE-complete. The hard positions have Alice to move first and both stores initially empty. The same positions are hard under either common convention for capture opposite an empty pit, and with or without the bonus rule, which gives a player another turn when the last stone is sown into their own store. We introduce Line Kalah as an intermediate problem, a game on a line in which stones that leave the line effectively disappear and Alice must save each of her target pits before Bob captures it, and we reduce quantified Boolean formulas to it. The reduction uses a set of sequential timer piles whose last stones approach a group of targets, forcing Alice to choose between two captures in order to set the truth value of a variable, and a final capture gadget to test a clause chosen by Bob (only one is needed adversarially). Since either player may move any pile at any time, the stages are placed so that premature timer firings protect earlier potential targets. For a true formula, Alice's strategy against arbitrary opposing play either gains enough time to save the remaining targets (after Bob deviates from the intended play) or reaches the final test with a correctly encoded, protected input. Finally, the line positions are embedded in Kalah with both stores empty. A separate Bob pit holds the score adjustment, so the winner takes a strict majority of the stones.
item.dc:creator: Ethan Dickey, Ethan Mader

item.title: Two-Stage Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programming in Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.14837v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lenstra showed that mixed-integer linear programming can be solved in polynomial time when the number of integer variables is fixed and the number of continuous variables is arbitrary. Mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) can be solved in polynomial time when the total number of variables is fixed. However, since MIQP is NP-hard already without integer variables, the analog of Lenstra's result fails unless P = NP. Hence, polynomial-time algorithms for MIQP with an arbitrary number of continuous variables must exploit additional structure. We study MIQPs with two-stage structure, which underlies Benders decomposition and two-stage stochastic programming. A few linking variables, including all integer variables, are coupled with many blocks of continuous variables that interact only through them, both in the constraints and in the objective. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for MIQP with an arbitrary quadratic objective when the number of linking variables and the block size are fixed, while the number of blocks, and hence the number of variables, is arbitrary. The case with no blocks is MIQP in fixed dimension. None of our assumptions can be dropped. Unless P = NP, the number of linking variables and the block size must both be fixed, the blocks cannot interact or contain integer variables, and large blocks cannot be allowed even if their objective is linear. Unless FPT = W[1], the exponent of the running time must depend on both the number of linking variables and the block size.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Del Pia

item.title: Almost Optimal Lower Bounds under Almost ETH for Approximating Euclidean k-means
item.description: arXiv:2611.14892v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the Euclidean $k$-means problem, we are given a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the goal is to find $k$ representative points in space so as to minimize the sum of the squared distances from each point to its closest representative. Algorithmically, de la Vega, Karpinski, Kenyon, and Rabani [STOC'03] and Kumar, Sabharwal, and Sen [JACM'10] obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for high-dimensional Euclidean $k$-means in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{O(1)}} \cdot dn^{O(1)}$, which was subsequently improved to $2^{\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)} + O(ndk)$ by Feldman, Monemizadeh, and Sohler [SoCG'07]. On the lower-bound side, a recent work of Cohen-Addad, Karthik, Saulpic, and Schwiegelshohn [SoCG'26] proposed the Exponential Time for Expanders Hypothesis (XXH), which asserts exponential-time hardness for $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximating Vertex Cover on vertex expanders, and used it to prove nearly matching running time lower bound whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$. We observe that XXH does not hold in the parameter regime needed for the above result, and show how to repair their reduction under a more standard assumption. More precisely, we show that assuming the Almost Exponential Time Hypothesis for 3-SAT (Almost ETH), for every constant $\beta\in(0,1)$, Euclidean $k$-means in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{1-\beta}}\text{poly}(n,d)$, whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$. By modifying the construction, we also obtain a similar result for approximating the Euclidean $k$-median problem.
item.dc:creator: Karthik C. S., Dor Minzer

item.title: Tokenization: Hardness and Bicriteria Approximation Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2611.15074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study Binary Tokenization: given a corpus of binary strings over $\{0,1\}$ and a vocabulary budget $K$, select at most $K$ substrings (called vocabulary) to minimize the total number of tokens needed to represent the corpus. The primitive symbols $0$ and $1$ are always available, and each document must be segmented separately. Letting $n$ denote the total corpus length and $M$ for the maximum document length, we prove that, for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, Binary Tokenization problem does not have polynomial-time $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation algorithms unless $\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{NP}$. To complement the hardness result, we give a polynomial-time $(\gamma,\gamma)$-bicriteria algorithm, with $\gamma = \sqrt{M}\log n$: The algorithm outputs a vocabulary of size at most $\gamma K$ with number of tokens at most $\gamma {\rm OPT}_K$, where ${\rm OPT}_K$ is the optimal number of tokens under the original budget $K$. We also study a storage-budget variant, in which the sum of the selected substrings' lengths is bounded by $B$. For $2\le B<n$, we obtain an $(O(\log n\log B),O(\log n\log B))$-bicriteria approximation algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Atieh Bastan, Xiaoling He, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran

item.title: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps
item.description: arXiv:2611.15128v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reed-Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations. For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius. We prove smaller error bounds using affine combiners, which combine two received words $f,g$ as $f(x)+(\alpha+\beta x)g(x)$, where $\alpha,\beta$ are independent uniform elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$. For output degree bound $d=\rho n$, fixed $\rho\in(0,1)$ and $0<\eta<1-\sqrt{\rho}$, and sufficiently large block length $n$, we prove mutual correlated agreement (MCA) with one coordinate of agreement loss at threshold $A=\lceil(\sqrt{\rho}+\eta)n\rceil$, with error $O_{\rho,\eta}\left(\frac{1}{q}+\frac{n^2}{q^2}\right)$. The result holds over arbitrary evaluation domains in every finite field, including prime and binary extension fields. The agreement threshold can approach the Johnson threshold, beyond unique decoding. For $q\ge n^2$, our error is $O_{\rho,\eta}(1/q)$, an asymptotic factor-$n$ separation from scalar combiners: we prove that their worst-case MCA error is $\Omega_{\rho,\eta}(n/q)$ at the same agreement threshold and with the same one-coordinate loss. We also prove that affine combiners incur worst-case error $\Omega_{\rho,\eta}(n/q)$ when no agreement loss is allowed. Thus one coordinate of agreement loss is necessary for our guarantee; this relaxation of standard MCA reduces the guaranteed common agreement fraction by at most $1/n$. We also extend the result to $k$-variate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids, obtaining MCA error $O_{\rho,\eta,k}(q^{-k})$ for fixed $\rho,\eta,k$, sufficiently large $n$, and $q\ge n^{k+1}$, with agreement loss $n^{1-1/k}$.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Chiesa, Guy Weissenberg, Eylon Yogev, Kai Zhe Zheng

item.title: Small Maximum Likelihood on Fixed Cavender-Farris-Neyman Trees: An Approximation Scheme and Limits to Fully Polynomial Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15784v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small Maximum Likelihood fits the edge substitution probabilities of a given phylogenetic tree to an observed alignment, summing over the unobserved ancestral states. For the binary Cavender--Farris--Neyman model, we assume a uniform root and an edge-specific substitution probability $p_e\in[0,\tfrac12]$ for each edge $e$, shared across all alignment sites. We give a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme. The algorithm achieves a factor of $1+\varepsilon$ for both the negative log likelihood and the loss after subtracting the uniform-root contribution. Its main step fixes ancestral sequences at one periodically spaced class of depths while summing over all remaining ancestors. A posterior entropy bound controls the cost of this restriction, and dynamic programming optimizes the resulting components over a finite parameter grid. We also give a randomized reduction from Clique showing that an FPTAS returning feasible rational edge probabilities would imply $RP=NP$. These results separate fixed-accuracy approximation from fully polynomial approximation for the same fixed-tree model.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad-Hadi Foroughmand-Araabi, Sama Goliaei

item.title: Statistical-to-computational gaps in central limit theorems for high-dimensional tensors
item.description: arXiv:2611.15803v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study high-dimensional central limit theorems (CLTs) as hypothesis testing problems, comparing the number of summands needed for statistical and computational indistinguishability of the normalized sum from the limiting Gaussian distribution as the dimension and number of summands grow together. For the off-diagonal entries of sums of i.i.d. rank-one tensors formed from standard Gaussian vectors (equivalently, the problem of distinguishing Wigner from Wishart tensors), we prove total variation bounds sharpening previous estimates of Mikulincer (2020) and give matching polynomial-time tests. This shows that the statistical and computational thresholds coincide for this CLT, contrary to a proposal by Kunisky, Moore, and Wein (2024). On the other hand, we also show that, for tensors of order at least three, sufficient Gaussian dilution of the summands by adding independent Gaussian noise and rescaling gives a CLT model with a statistical-to-computational gap (in the above setting and ones with more general rank-one summand distributions). To the best of our knowledge, such a phenomenon has not been observed before in any high-dimensional CLT. In particular, in the relevant parameter regimes, we show that a brute-force search achieves strong detection, while polynomials of degree up to $n^{\Omega(1)}$ cannot achieve strong separation. The latter lower bounds control low-degree $\chi^2$-divergences by a novel method based on cumulant generating functions, and we further illustrate the use of these tools by applying them to masked tensor CLT models where only a prescribed subset of tensor entries is revealed.
item.dc:creator: Debsurya De, Dmitriy Kunisky

item.title: Individually Fair Facility Location
item.description: arXiv:2611.16138v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study individually fair facility location, where each client must connect to an open facility within a prescribed radius and the objective is to minimize total opening and connection cost. We show that preserving the radii changes the approximability of metric facility location fundamentally. For every fixed radius violation below three, no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm achieves a sublogarithmic cost factor unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. The hardness holds with uniform opening costs and uniform radii. It contradicts the strict-fairness constant-factor guarantee recently claimed by Liu, Xu, and Zhang [Theory of Computing Systems, Vol. 70 (2026)]. We then establish a positive result for arbitrary client radii. We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that has cost at most $1.725$ times the strictly fair optimum and serves every client within three times its fair radius (in the Appendix we show how this can be de-randomized). We use the approach of Byrka, Srinivasan and Swamy [IPCO 2010]. The facility-location radius factor three is therefore optimal among deterministic polynomial-time algorithms with constant cost factor, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. Experiments on real-world data indicate that the worst case radius bound is rarely realized in practice: the algorithm serves over 99.8% of clients within their stated radius, and never beyond 1.5 times it. Our code is available at https://github.com/milindmaiti/IFFL_Implementation.
item.dc:creator: Rajni Dabas, Samir Khuller, Milind Maiti

item.title: Tight Algorithms for Conservative Finite-Valued CSPs Parameterized by Treewidth
item.description: arXiv:2611.16729v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider valued constraint satisfaction problems (VCSPs) with a fixed finite domain $D$ and a fixed finite constraint language $\Gamma$, in the setting where $\Gamma$ contains all crisp unary constraints (called hard lists) and the remaining cost functions are finite-valued. We call such a language a finite-valued hard-list language. Let $c_\Gamma$ be the size of the largest set $S\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ can express (using the usual VCSP closure operations) a binary disequality function on elements of $S$. Our main result tightly connects the complexity of the problem parameterized by treewidth to this value $c_\Gamma$. (1) The problem can be solved in time $(c_\Gamma)^{\mathsf{tw}} \cdot (|I| + |\mathcal{T}|)^{O(1)}$ when given an instance $I$ with a tree decomposition $\mathcal{T}$ of width $\mathsf{tw}$ of the primal graph of $I$. (2) If $c_\Gamma \geq 2$, there is no such algorithm solving the problem in time $(c_\Gamma - \varepsilon)^{\mathsf{tw}} \cdot (|I| + |\mathcal{T}|)^{O(1)}$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$, unless the Primal Treewidth SETH (and hence CNF-SETH) fails. In particular, this gives a far-reaching generalization of a similar result of Esmer et al. [ESA 2024] on the optimization version of list homomorphism for graphs.
item.dc:creator: Jakob Greilhuber, D\'aniel Marx, George Osipov, Marta Piecyk, Pawe{\l} Rz\k{a}\.zewski, Stanislav \v{Z}ivn\'y

item.title: The Tournament Equilibrium Set Is PSPACE-Complete, Even under Hereditary Uniqueness
item.description: arXiv:2611.17312v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The tournament equilibrium set (TEQ), proposed by Schwartz in 1990, is a classical voting rule based on pairwise majority comparisons. Its definition is recursive: an alternative is judged by the alternatives that beat it, called its dominators, and by which of those dominators TEQ itself selects. Deciding whether a given alternative belongs to TEQ was known to be NP-hard and to lie in PSPACE. We close this gap by proving that the problem is PSPACE-complete. To our knowledge, this is the first PSPACE-completeness result for membership in a tournament solution. The hardness persists even when every nonempty subtournament has a unique minimal retentive set, the property conjectured by Schwartz to hold for all tournaments. Moreover, every such subtournament in our hard instances contains an alternative with at most three dominators. We prove that a single alternative with at most four dominators suffices both to guarantee uniqueness and to find a TEQ winner in $O(N^2)$ time. Thus, on our hard instances, finding one winner is efficient even though recognizing a specified winner is PSPACE-complete. We also study how the complexity changes with the dominator bound. If every nonempty subtournament has an alternative with at most one dominator, the entire TEQ can be computed in quadratic time; allowing two dominators makes membership NP-hard. Under the same condition with four dominators, all $t$ winners can be computed in $O(2^t N^2)$ time, where $N$ is the number of alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Ethan Dickey, Athina Terzoglou

item.title: An even simpler hard variant of Not-All-Equal 3-SAT
item.description: arXiv:2412.03395v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat under a strong structural restriction and delineate a sharp tractability threshold. In particular, we consider the restriction of Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat to instances that simultaneously satisfy the following properties: (i) the clauses can be decomposed into a disjoint union of $k$ partitions of the variable set, and (ii) the collection of clauses is linear, that is, each pair of distinct clauses shares at most one variable. We show that, under these conditions, Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat remains NP-complete for any fixed $k \geq 4$. On the positive side, we prove that for $k \leq 3$, the problem is in P and, notably, all such instances are not-all-equal-satisfiable. Our results do not only show robustness of NP-completeness despite the strong structure imposed but also have implications for hypergraph coloring. In particular, by the well-known correspondence between Positive Not-All-Equal 3-Sat and hypergraph coloring, we obtain the following corollary of our results: For $k\geq 4$, Bicolorability is NP-complete for linear 3-uniform $k$-regular hypergraphs even if the edges are given as a decomposition into $k$ perfect matchings; with the same restrictions, for $k \leq 3$ Bicolorability is in P, and all such hypergraphs are bicolorable. In addition, we show that loosening the restriction to 3-clauses by also allowing 2-clauses shifts the above-mentioned tractability threshold. Moreover, we deduce that every instance of Positive Planar Not-All-Equal Sat with at least three distinct variables per clause is nae-satisfiable. Besides, for Linear Not-All-Equal 3-Sat we derive a computational complexity dichotomy with respect to the number of variable appearances.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Darmann, Janosch D\"ocker, Britta Dorn

item.title: On the Reachability Problem on Monoid-Labelled Undirected Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2606.21103v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The labelled reachability problem for undirected graphs with edges labelled by elements of a monoid $M$ (more generally, groupoids or magmas) captures the classes $\sf{L}$ and $\sf{NL}$. Given a graph $G(V, E)$ labelled by $\phi~\colon E \to M$, $s,t \in V$ and an accepting subset $F \subseteq M$, the problem asks to test whether there is a walk $P$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ where $\phi(P) \in F$. Ramaswamy et al. (2019) studied the variant where the accepting element is part of the input for aperiodic monoids and groups. Motivated by the success in designing space-bounded algorithms for the undirected graph reachability problem, we study the labelled reachability problem when the accepting set is also fixed. This reveals finer complexity bounds and dichotomies for the problem based on the monoid and the accepting set. Previous results imply that the problem is in $\sf{L}$ for any finite accepting subset when $M$ is a group or belongs to $\sf{DA}$. We prove the following (for finite monoids): 1) For any monoid $M$, the problem is in $\sf{L}$ when the accepting element is the identity of $M$. If the accepting element is an idempotent, under suitable constraints, the problem is $\sf{NL}$-hard. 2) For any commutative monoid $M$, the problem is in $\sf{L}$ for all $F \subseteq M$. 3) For any $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{R})$-commutative union-of-groups (UoG) monoid $M$, the problem is in $\sf{L}$ for all $F\subseteq M$. We show deterministic logspace algorithms for UoG monoids that are neither $\mathcal{L}$-commutative nor $\mathcal{R}$-commutative, under certain constraints. 4) For the monoids $\sf{BA_2}$ and $\sf{U}$, we show a dichotomy: for all $F \subseteq M$, the problem is either $\sf{NL}$-complete or in $\sf{L}$. Our results exploit the connection between Green's relations in the UoG monoids and the properties of the product graph (a graph introduced by Ramaswamy et al. (2019)).
item.dc:creator: Nagashri Krishnakumar, Harshil Mittal, Jayalal Sarma

item.title: Interactive Proofs of Proximity for Model Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2609.32007v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study interactive proofs of proximity (IPPs) for model evaluation, where a resource-limited verifier interacts with an untrusted prover, typically the model owner, to certify statistical properties of a model under an unknown input distribution. Our formulation separates sampling the input distribution from querying the model and evaluating its output; distinguishes real audit data (black-box sampling) from generated data (chosen-randomness, or gray-box, access to the sampler); and allows the prover and verifier to use different evaluators. We focus on doubly-sublinear IPPs, where both the verifier and honest prover use sublinear resources, and on (weighted) Hamming weight properties. For ordinary Hamming weight, we give a tolerant doubly-sublinear IPP. For completeness and soundness radii $\varepsilon_c<\varepsilon_f$ and gap $g=\varepsilon_f-\varepsilon_c$, a logarithmic-round instantiation uses $\widetilde{O}(1/g)$ verifier queries and $O(1/g^2)$ honest-prover queries, improving the cubic dependence of Amir, Goldreich, and Rothblum (ITCS 2025). We prove matching query lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. For distribution-weighted Hamming weight, black-box sampling requires $\Theta(1/g^2)$ verifier samples but only $\widetilde{O}(1/g)$ evaluations; the quadratic sample complexity is necessary in the interior regime. With chosen-randomness access, the problem reduces to ordinary Hamming weight, yielding $\widetilde{O}(1/g)$ calls and evaluations. If the parties' evaluators disagree arbitrarily on a $\rho$-fraction of the distribution and by at most $\gamma$ elsewhere, our protocols remain doubly sublinear whenever $g>2\kappa$, where $\kappa=\rho+(1-\rho)\gamma$. Applications include auditing accuracy, group fairness, calibration, harmlessness, usefulness, and average-case robustness.
item.dc:creator: Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolas Melissaris, Tamara Paris

item.title: Asymptotic Rank of Weighted Graph Tensors via Completely Positive Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.34273v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a conic upper bound on the asymptotic rank of every weighted graph tensor over every field. If $W$ is the logarithmic edge-weight matrix of its dimension matrix $Q$, then $$ \operatorname{MaxCut}(W)\le\log_2\operatorname{\widetilde R}_{\mathbb F}(\mathsf{WT}(Q))\le U_{\operatorname{CP}}^{\Delta}(W). $$ Here $U_{\operatorname{CP}}^{\Delta}(W)$ maximizes $\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}W_{i,j}P_{i,j}$ over nonnegative symmetric zero-diagonal matrices $P$ such that $J-2P$ is copositive and $P_{i,j}\le P_{i,k}+P_{k,j}$ for all distinct vertices. The matrix $J$ is all-one, and copositivity means nonnegativity of the quadratic form on nonnegative vectors. Our starting point extends OpenAI's polynomial multiplication method and its subsequent arbitrary-field developments from three tensor legs to arbitrary order. We prove $$ \left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor\le\log_2\operatorname{\widetilde R}_{\mathbb F}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))\le\frac{n^2}{4}. $$ The edge exponent is at most $n/(2(n-1))$ and tends to the optimal value $1/2$, improving the previous Coppersmith--Winograd bounds and answering Question 1.3.1 of Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam. The bounds coincide for every even $n$. For every odd $m\ge3$, the theorem gives $\log_2\widetilde R_{\mathbb F}(\mathsf{GT}_2(C_m))\le m-1+1/(m+1)$, improving the previous cycle bound with a gap of only $1/(m+1)$ above the maximum cut. On weighted triangles, the program recovers the rectangular matrix multiplication curve of Uzna'nski and Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam. The CP and semidefinite programs, with or without path constraints, all have value $9/4$ on the unweighted triangle, giving this upper bound a natural conic interpretation. Further applications give explicit bounds for complete multipartite graphs, split graphs, and wheels, including new cases of maximum-cut equality.
item.dc:creator: Huanyi Zhou

item.title: The determinantal complexity of the 4*4 permanent is 15
item.description: arXiv:2611.06658v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The best known lower bound on the determinantal complexity of the 4x4 permanent is 10. In this short note, I prove that this value is exactly 15: the 4x4 permanent is the determinant of a 15x15 matrix of affine linear forms, and cannot be that of any smaller matrix. To do so, I must establish both a lower and upper bound. To establish the upper bound, I use Grenet's construction of size 2^n-1. Hence that construction is optimal at n=4 (and n=3). This now constitutes the first knwon exact value of the determinantal complexity of the permanent at n=4. Only the value at n=3 was exactly known, prior to this note. The general quadratic bound only gives 8 for n=4. To establish the lower bound, I work from a normal form at a zero of the permanent. In the first row (and column) of the normal form, the linear forms vanish on a linear space inside the singular locus of the permanent. A hessian inequality bounds the size of the matrix in terms of that space. Then, a matrix of sie 14 foces the space into any of nine corordinate types. The forcing is either up to symmetry, or else into a family that degenerates to one of them. I then rule out every case. All involved computations are exact. In respect of the claim, I have made all certificates public.

item.title: Near-Quadratic Time Multivariate Polynomial Interpolation
item.description: arXiv:2610.30907v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $\F$ be a finite field. Given $N$ distinct points $\bm{\alpha}_1,\ldots,\bm{\alpha}_N \in \F^m$ and associated values $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_N \in \F$, we study the problem of computing an $m$-variate polynomial $f(\vy) \in \F[\vy]$ of individual degree less than $d$, with $d^m \ge N$, that satisfies $f(\bm{\alpha}_i)=\beta_i$ for all $i\in[N]$, whenever such an $f$ exists. This is known as the\textit{ multivariate polynomial interpolation} problem. In this work, given $N=d^m$, we present a deterministic algorithm for multivariate polynomial interpolation over an arbitrary finite field $\F$ that runs in near-quadratic time $N^{2+o(1)}\poly(m,d,\log|\F|)$, assuming $d$ is $\omega(1)$. This bound holds whenever the associated \emph{multivariate Vandermonde} matrix is nonsingular, has constant co-rank, or admits some special structure. In the general case, we give a randomized Las Vegas algorithm attaining the same near-quadratic running time, provided the finite field is sufficiently large and $d$ grows similar to the previous case. Unlike other multivariate interpolation strategies, we do not assume black-box access to the polynomial. In particular, we are not permitted to query arbitrary input points to obtain their evaluations. Our interpolation result follows by combining Wiedemann's classical approach~\cite{w86} for solving sparse linear systems with known bounds for fast \emph{multivariate multipoint evaluation} over finite fields~\cite{umans08, KU11, BGKM23, BGGKU24}. Specifically, our deterministic interpolation strategy relies on a deterministic variant of Wiedemann's approach, which is more commonly used in the randomized setting.
item.dc:creator: Chandra Kanta Mohapatra

item.title: Community Search under Member-Specific Tolerances
item.description: arXiv:2611.05951v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study community search when each member has its own tolerance for differences in position, as when members of a group interact repeatedly and influence one another. A latitude-consistent community (LCC) contains the query vertex, is connected, has minimum degree at least k, and bounds its diameter by the smallest member tolerance. The bound is exactly the condition under which every interaction in a connected closed group stays accepted under bounded-confidence dynamics for every choice of positive weights. It also prevents rejection under social-judgment dynamics, whereas the pairwise condition and other natural relaxations preserve neither guarantee. Finding a maximum LCC is NP-hard even in the plane, and with unbounded dimension, deciding whether an LCC exists is NP-complete for every fixed k>=2. LatSweep fixes the answer's smallest tolerance and turns the coupled bound into a best-first sweep over candidate thresholds, yielding an exact branch-and-bound algorithm, a (1,2)-bicriteria approximation and two feasible heuristics. Across eight graphs with up to 1.8 billion edges, six with synthetic positions and tolerances, the exact algorithm proves optimality on all but 9 of 3,700 efficiency queries; in a shared implementation on two large graphs, its branch-and-bound solver proves more queries than a reimplemented maximum-(k,r)-core algorithm, a mixed-integer program and CP-SAT. In simulations of closed groups, LCC groups keep every accepted interaction under uneven influence, whereas 3-40% of pairwise-compatible groups lose some. On three location-based networks, tolerance-agnostic groups often place another member's home beyond a member's estimated travel radius. Enforcing every member's tolerance causes no measurable loss of co-visits relative to spatial communities of the same size. Relative to the larger pairwise-compatible groups, it can cause a size-adjusted loss.
item.dc:creator: Yanghao Liu, Fangda Guo, Yuxuan Zhang, Xueqi Cheng
